BXL-2425-00018-v1.headline: Let cafés and restaurants keep their Covid-era street terraces all year round, permanently, without needing a planning permit.
BXL-2425-00018-v1.proposed_by: Ludivine de Magnanville (MR), co-signed by Pascal Smet (Vooruit.brussels), Isabelle Emmery (PS), Lotte Stoops (Groen) and others across several groups
BXL-2425-00018-v1.source_brief:
During the Covid lockdowns Brussels permitted café and restaurant owners to set up terraces in public space without a planning permit, as a lifeline for a sector forbidden from trading indoors. Those rules proved popular and were extended repeatedly by a caretaker government — most recently to 31 December 2025. This resolution urges the incoming government to write the exemption into the standing permit-dispensation decree permanently, so operators have the legal certainty to invest properly in their terrace infrastructure.

- **Who it touches:** independent bar, café and restaurant owners across Brussels, particularly those on narrow streets or with small frontages who relied on the extra outdoor space to survive the pandemic and now fear a return to heavy administrative procedures.
- **The legal mechanism:** operators would still need a communal horeca licence and a road-occupation authorisation; municipalities retain the power to impose conditions (including seasonal limits) and to withdraw authorisation. Only the planning-permit requirement for the structure itself would go.
- **The nuance:** supporters note the existing circular included other benefits — wider footpaths, greening, cycle infrastructure — and some members call for those gains to be carried into the permanent framework, so the reform is not just about terraces.
- **The rub:** whether entrenching year-round terrace rights strikes the right balance between supporting a fragile sector and protecting pedestrian access, wheelchair users, and genuinely shared public space.
deep_facts: The Brussels government issued guidelines in 2021 authorising horeca operators to install public-space terraces year-round without a planning permit (permis d'urbanisme), as a response to the Covid-19 economic crisis (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

The measures were originally planned for two years; they were subsequently extended to 30 September 2024, then again — by the caretaker government — to 31 December 2025, creating a succession of temporary extensions that the sector found unsatisfactory for long-term investment planning (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

The resolution asks the government to amend the existing arrête on planning-permit dispensations to incorporate a permanent, year-round terrace authorisation, in conformity with the current guidelines, removing the need for further case-by-case extensions (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

Operators retaining obligations include: a communal horeca exploitation authorisation and a communal or regional road-occupation authorisation; municipalities may still impose seasonality conditions, financial guarantees, or other requirements, and may withdraw authorisation for non-compliance (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

Proponents argue that the temporary nature of successive extensions has deterred operators from investing in quality permanent terrace infrastructure; legal certainty through a permanent rule would unlock those investments (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

A speaker from Groen flagged that the 2021 circular contained wider benefits — simplified greening, widened footpaths and cycle paths, improved pedestrian crossings — that are not automatically carried over and should be integrated into the permanent urban-planning framework, specifically in the forthcoming Good Living regional regulation (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

Accessibility concerns were raised: expanding terraces in public space has at times made wheelchair navigation more difficult; the permanent framework must preserve an unobstructed pedestrian passage, and communes are urged to take their enforcement responsibilities seriously (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).
The resolution went through the committee on Territorial Development before being brought to plenary; a PS-tabled amendment by Pascal Smet contributed to that consensus (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

Speakers across groups cited the broader economic fragility of Brussels — the president of the French-language commercial court had just told the economics committee that business failures were accelerating across all sectors — as context for why legislative certainty for horeca mattered urgently (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).
BXL-2425-00018-v1.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The cross-party tone of the committee work and the plenary debate signals that this is one of the rare files where the left-right divide disappears: supporting small independent traders and removing red tape are framing devices that work across the ideological spectrum simultaneously.
- The caretaker government's repeated one-year extensions are the practical driver: each extension creates a planning horizon too short for a terrace investment to pay back, so the sector kept lobbying. Making the rule permanent is less a policy choice than a bureaucratic fix everyone can agree on.
- The Groen amendment folding in greening and pedestrian access is the only real tension point — it reframes the text from a pure deregulation measure into a modest public-space-quality requirement, which is why it found majority support but is framed as a long-term ask rather than a blocking condition.
- The timing — voted the same morning as the far more divisive rent ordinance — underscores how different the political temperature can be on two housing-adjacent files decided on the same day.
BXL-2425-00018-v1.raw_fr: La proposition de résolution invite le gouvernement à modifier de manière permanente l'arrêté relatif aux dispenses de permis d'urbanisme, afin d'autoriser l'installation de terrasses horeca dans l'espace public toute l'année, dans le respect des lignes directrices existantes. Ces mesures, introduites en 2021 dans le contexte de la pandémie de Covid-19, ont été prorogées à plusieurs reprises à titre provisoire, créant une insécurité juridique préjudiciable aux investissements du secteur. Le texte maintient les obligations d'autorisation communale et d'occupation de voirie, ainsi que les prérogatives des communes en matière de conditions et de retrait d'autorisation.

BXL-2425-00018-v4.headline: Give Brussels tenants the right to take an abusive rent to a judge and have it lowered, starting 1 May 2025 — activating a law voted in 2021 but never switched on.
BXL-2425-00018-v4.proposed_by: Martin Casier (PS), Kalvin Soiresse Njall (Ecolo), Stijn Bex (Groen), Nadia El Yousfi (PS), Farida Tahar (Ecolo), Mohamed Ouriaghli (PS), Ilyas Mouani (Vooruit.brussels), Françoise De Smedt (PTB), Jan Busselen (PVDA), Fouad Ahidar (Team Fouad Ahidar)
BXL-2425-00018-v4.source_brief:
In October 2021 the Brussels Parliament passed an ordinance creating a joint rental commission (Commission paritaire locative) to tackle abusive rents, but left articles 8–13 — the ones giving tenants a right of action before a justice of the peace — without an entry-into-force date. This ordinance sets that date as 1 May 2025. The session was one of the most dramatic in recent Brussels parliamentary history: an agenda-change vote that very morning forced the text onto the day's schedule; opposition parties argued the supporting rent reference grid is too old and unrepresentative; an amendment to delay activation to 1 January 2027 was put to a vote; and after its defeat, part of the opposition walked out in a quorum-breaking manoeuvre that suspended the sitting for 40 minutes.

- **What articles 8–13 do:** a tenant whose rent exceeds the indicative reference rent by more than 20% AND who faces qualifying quality defects in the property can petition the Commission paritaire locative for a conciliation opinion, then use that opinion before a justice of the peace to seek a rent reduction.
- **The grid dispute:** opponents argued the reference rent grid is built on data collected in 2017–2020, making it unrepresentative of 2025 market conditions; proponents cited updated indexation and a researcher-confirmed sample of 3,000-plus observations as sufficient.
- **The walkout:** after the 2027-delay amendment was rejected, an opposition leader called a suspension on quorum grounds and several opposition groups’ deputies left the chamber; after a 40-minute suspension, quorum was restored and the vote proceeded.
- **The rub:** whether activating a mechanism tied to a contested reference grid protects Brussels tenants — around 60% of the population — from abusive landlords, or whether it risks chilling investment in a market already starved of new supply.
deep_facts: The 2021 ordonnance (28 October 2021) was adopted with only four votes against; articles 8 to 13, which organise the judicial action for rent revision before the justice of the peace, were left without an entry-into-force date pending a political agreement that the previous government never concluded (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

Articles 8–13 define the Commission paritaire locative's role as issuing a binding advisory opinion (avis) that a tenant can use as the basis for a judicial claim; the Commission is parity-based — equal representation of landlords and tenants — and speakers noted that of the three dossiers processed to date, two were rejected as not constituting abusive rents (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

The abusive-rent trigger has two cumulative criteria: the rent must exceed the indicative reference rent by more than 20%, AND quality defects in the property must be established; a high-quality property exceeding the median by 20% is not automatically classified as abusive (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

The indicative rent reference grid (grille des loyers) was originally built on data from 2017, 2018 and 2020; it has since been updated by indexation and a new statistical methodology developed by researcher Hugo Périlleux; Périlleux testified in committee that a sample of 3,000 to 4,000 observations is statistically sufficient for the new approach (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

Key statistics cited in the debate: median Brussels rents rose 143% since 2018 compared to a health-index rise of roughly 20-23%; 10% of Brussels residents with the lowest incomes spend an average of 45% of their income on housing (Baromètre social 2023); some households spend up to 70% (Rassemblement bruxellois pour le droit à l'habitat); the social housing waiting list exceeds 60,000 households; an estimated 7,000 to 10,000 people are homeless (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

MR speaker de Clippele cited estimates from the developer Hugo Périlleux of 70,000 potentially affected properties, and cited 2025 rental-advertisement data showing 95% of listings on Immoweb, Immovlan and Logic-Immo exceeding the reference rent by more than 20%, raising concern about the mechanism's effective scope (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

DéFI and Open Vld filed amendment no. 1 to article 2, replacing '1 mai 2025' with '1er janvier 2027', arguing that an additional 20 months would allow the regional lease-registration system — which had already collected more than 5,000 leases in three months — to produce a reliably representative grid; the amendment was rejected (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

After the amendment was defeated, MR group leader Barzin called a suspension on quorum grounds; MR, N-VA and Vlaams Belang deputies then left the chamber; the sitting was suspended from 17h47 to 18h29; quorum was reached after the suspension and the article-2 and whole-text votes proceeded with 61 members present (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

The morning sitting (séance n° 17) had begun with PS leader Laaouej requesting an agenda change under article 52 of the standing orders to add the ordonnance to the same day's plenary; that procedural vote carried despite objections from several opposition groups on grounds of undue haste and insufficient hearings (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).

An economics professor (Prof. Sven Damen) testified in committee that international studies on rent-control regimes consistently show four side effects: reduced supply, lower housing quality, reduced household mobility, and a halt in new construction; opposition speakers cited Berlin's 2020 rent cap, struck down by the Federal Constitutional Court in 2021, as a cautionary parallel (CRI, 4 Apr 2025).
BXL-2425-00018-v4.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The 2027-delay amendment is the real strategic contest: it was not a wrecking amendment but a genuine offer to the swing votes (DéFI, Open Vld, Les Engagés), and the majority's refusal to accept it forced those groups to choose between a mechanism they helped design in 2021 and an entry-into-force they consider premature — most ended up voting no on the amendment but staying for the final vote, which is exactly the 'democratic courtesy' PS leader Laaouej thanked them for.
- The quorum walkout is the most revealing moment: it signals that MR and allies judged the political cost of being recorded as voting against a tenant-protection measure at roll call to be higher than the reputational cost of a walkout, which they calculated would be framed as a procedural objection rather than an ideological one.
- The grid-reliability debate is technically unresolved. Both sides cite credentialed experts; the underlying disagreement is whether a statistically adequate sample justifies activating a legally binding mechanism when the underlying rent data predate the pandemic. That question will likely return in any post-implementation litigation.
- The absence of a full government for ten months is load-bearing context: the majority coalition acted precisely because they feared that a new government including parties hostile to rent regulation might repeal or indefinitely delay articles 8–13, making the parliamentary window a now-or-never moment.
BXL-2425-00018-v4.raw_fr: La proposition d'ordonnance fixe au 1er mai 2025 l'entrée en vigueur des articles 8 à 13 de l'ordonnance du 28 octobre 2021, qui organisent une action en révision de loyer abusif devant le juge de paix, sur la base d'un avis de la Commission paritaire locative. Ces articles étaient restés sans date d'entrée en vigueur depuis 2021 faute d'accord politique. Le texte a été inscrit à l'ordre du jour en urgence le matin même, à la suite d'un vote procédural ; un amendement proposant de reporter l'entrée en vigueur au 1er janvier 2027 a été rejeté ; la séance a été suspendue quarante minutes après une tentative de rupture du quorum, avant que le vote final ne soit acquis.
